Research task: Identify all plausible historical-fiction novels (or commonly-labeled Victorian-set fiction, including originals if the term is loosely applied) published before 2017, set primarily in 19th-century London, that match the following detailed plot beats: (a) the protagonist is in disguise; (b) they help a businessman (merchant/financier/industrialist) avert or avoid a disastrous deal; (c) the protagonist is wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document; (d) the real culprit is a schemer planning to send the encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad; (e) climax involves a fierce sea storm in which the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist, securing their safety.

Instructions:
- Use targeted searches combining distinctive terms and synonyms: "Victorian London" + disguise + businessman + "stolen document" + secret papers/cipher/encrypted + "send abroad" + storm/sea/ship rescue; also try broader combinations and quotation searches.
- For each candidate you find: provide title, author, original publication year, genre label (historical fiction vs original period fiction), setting details (confirm 19th-century London as a primary setting), and a bullet list mapping the five plot beats to evidence from reliable sources (publisher blurb, detailed synopsis, reviews, wikis, library catalogs). Include citation links.
- If only partial matches occur (e.g., secret papers but no sea storm, or disguise but not businessman), include the candidate anyway with clear notes on mismatches/uncertainties.
- Consider well-known Victorian mysteries and modern historical mysteries/novels: Wilkie Collins, Dickens, Sarah Waters, Anne Perry, Michael Cox, Anthony Horowitz (Sherlockian), etc., but remain open to YA/adventure and lesser-known titles. Also check Holmes stories like "Naval Treaty"/"Bruce-Partington Plans" (note: short stories, not novels) and flag format mismatches.
- Return a structured summary with multiple candidates, each with linked evidence and explicit uncertainties. Aim for completeness over early filtering.

Research expansion summary and final answer Overview This session investigated seven candidate works against a specified five-beat plot test. For each title, I collected authoritative bibliographic details and plot overviews (from Wikipedia, library catalogs such as WorldCat, and public-domain sources like Project Gutenberg), then mapped evidence to the five beats: (i) protagonist in disguise (ii) helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal (iii) protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document (iv) a villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad (v) a climax with a fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist Result in brief: - None of the seven fully match all five beats. - Only A Spy in the House (Y. S. Lee) clearly satisfies (i) “protagonist in disguise” (undercover as a companion in a merchant’s home). - No clear evidence was found in reliable sources for (ii), (iii), (iv), (v) for any title. Process summary (high level) - Searched and scraped reliable sources for each candidate (Wikipedia where available; WorldCat for publisher summaries when Wikipedia pages were absent; Project Gutenberg for primary text of Mr. Meeson’s Will). - Confirmed title variants where applicable (e.g., Treason at Lisson Grove is the US title of Anne Perry’s Betrayal at Lisson Grove via Anne Perry’s Wikipedia bibliography). - Extracted plot details to test beats (i)–(v); flagged when no evidence was found. Final answer: per-title documentation and beat mapping 1) Mr. Meeson’s Will (H. Rider Haggard, 1888) - Title/author/year: - H. Rider Haggard, Mr. Meeson’s Will (1888). - Project Gutenberg (public-domain text & metadata): https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11913 - Early print records (e.g., 1888 Tauchnitz): https://search.worldcat.org/title/970930720 - Setting and genre: - Victorian England and at sea; shipboard on the R.M.S. Kangaroo; marooning in the southern Indian Ocean (Kerguelen/Desolation Island). Adventure fiction. - Primary text confirms the sea departure: “It was on a Tuesday evening that a mighty vessel was steaming… the steamship Kangaroo” (Ch. V): https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/11913/pg11913-images.html - Beat-by-beat: - (i) Protagonist in disguise: No evidence found in reliable sources/primary text excerpts. - (ii) Helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal: No evidence found. Early chapters depict exploitative dealings by publisher Meeson (Ch. I–II): https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/11913/pg11913-images.html - (iii) Protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document: No evidence found. The “will” plot centers on the famous tattoo-will episode after a shipwreck (see full text via Gutenberg main page: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11913). - (iv) Villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad: No evidence; the key “document” is the will (tattoo), not a cipher sent abroad. - (v) Climax with fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist: No evidence found in reliable summaries or the primary text passages reviewed. 2) A Spy in the House (Y. S. Lee, 2009) – The Agency #1 - Title/author/year: - Y. S. Lee, A Spy in the House (2009; U.S. ed. 2010). - WorldCat (1st U.S. ed. 2010; Candlewick summary): https://search.worldcat.org/title/863592991 - WorldCat (eBook summary with key line about disguise): https://search.worldcat.org/title/1083452785 - Setting and genre: - Victorian London (1850s); YA historical mystery/adventure (The Agency series). - Representative summary: “Rescued from the gallows in 1850s London… at seventeen, she infiltrates a rich merchant’s home in hopes of tracing his missing cargo ships.” - Beat-by-beat: - (i) Protagonist in disguise: Yes. “Assuming the guise of a lady’s companion, she must infiltrate a rich merchant’s home…” (WorldCat eBook summary): https://search.worldcat.org/title/1083452785 - (ii) Helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal: No evidence; the mission is to trace missing cargo ships via infiltration, not avert a specific disastrous deal. - (iii) Protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document: No evidence found. - (iv) Villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad: No evidence; the plot concerns smuggling/missing cargo, not ciphers shipped abroad. - (v) Climax with fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist: No evidence found. 3) The Last Dickens (Matthew Pearl, 2009) - Title/author/year: - Matthew Pearl, The Last Dickens (2009). Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Dickens - Setting and genre: - Historical/literary mystery set in the U.S., England, and India, 1867 and 1870. - Plot (Wikipedia): “When news of Charles Dickens’s untimely death… partner James R. Osgood sends his trusted clerk Daniel Sand to await Dickens’s unfinished last novel… Daniel’s body is discovered… Osgood must embark on a transatlantic quest to unearth the novel that will save his business…” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Dickens - Beat-by-beat: - (i) Protagonist in disguise: No evidence in the reliable summary. - (ii) Helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal: Partially related business stakes (“save his venerable business”) but does not match the “avert a disastrous deal” trope specified. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Dickens - (iii) Protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document: No evidence. - (iv) Villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad: No evidence; focuses on a missing manuscript rather than a cipher being shipped abroad. - (v) Climax with fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist: No evidence. 4) The Extraordinary and Unusual Adventures of Horatio Lyle (Catherine Webb, 2006) - Title/author/year: - Catherine Webb, The extraordinary and unusual adventures of Horatio Lyle (2006). - WorldCat record and summary: https://search.worldcat.org/title/67369661 - Setting and genre: - Victorian-set YA adventure/detective; Horatio Lyle is “a former Special Constable with a passion for science and invention… an occasional sleuth… [with] Tess… and Thomas… pursuing a dangerous enemy…” (WorldCat summary). - Beat-by-beat: - (i) Protagonist in disguise: No evidence in the summary. - (ii) Helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal: No evidence. - (iii) Protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document: No evidence. - (iv) Villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad: No evidence in summary. - (v) Climax with fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist: No evidence. 5) Treason at Lisson Grove (Anne Perry, 2011) [US title of Betrayal at Lisson Grove] - Title/author/year: - Anne Perry, Treason at Lisson Grove (US title of Betrayal at Lisson Grove), 2011. - Anne Perry’s Wikipedia bibliography confirms title variant: “Betrayal at Lisson Grove (US title: Treason at Lisson Grove) (2011)” under Thomas & Charlotte Pitt: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Perry - WorldCat listing with summary: https://search.worldcat.org/title/651902112 and expanded: https://search.worldcat.org/title/1132252501 - Setting and genre: - 1895; Special Branch political thriller/detective; pursuit from London to St. Malo (France), while Charlotte investigates in Dublin. - “Special Branch officer Thomas Pitt, hastening to rendezvous with a secret informant… a knife-wielding assassin… Pitt… pursues the killer… his wife Charlotte heads to Dublin to investigate…” (WorldCat: https://search.worldcat.org/title/651902112) - Beat-by-beat: - (i) Protagonist in disguise: No evidence. - (ii) Helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal: No; the plot focuses on political/terror intrigue. - (iii) Protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document: No; Narraway is accused over an informant’s death; no businessman/document-theft beat. - (iv) Villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad: No such detail in summaries. - (v) Climax with fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist: No evidence. 6) The Wrecker (Robert Louis Stevenson & Lloyd Osbourne, 1892) - Title/author/year: - Robert Louis Stevenson & Lloyd Osbourne, The Wrecker (1892). Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wrecker_(Stevenson_novel) - Setting and genre: - Adventure/detective; South Seas/Transpacific; revolves around “the abandoned wreck of the Flying Scud at Midway Atoll,” with detective elements via clues in a stamp collection. - Wikipedia: “It revolves around the abandoned wreck of the Flying Scud at Midway Atoll. Clues in a stamp collection are used to track down the missing crew and solve the mystery.” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wrecker_(Stevenson_novel) - Beat-by-beat: - (i) Protagonist in disguise: No evidence in reliable overview. - (ii) Helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal: No such beat in summary. - (iii) Protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document: No evidence. - (iv) Villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad: No evidence; documents are clues, not ciphers being shipped abroad. - (v) Climax with fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist: Not indicated in the summary. 7) The Quincunx (Charles Palliser, 1989/1990) - Title/author/year: - Charles Palliser, The Quincunx (The Inheritance of John Huffam), 1989 (UK). Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quincunx - Setting and genre: - Early 19th-century England; large-scale Dickensian historical mystery focused on inheritance, wills, and codicils. - Supporting plot excerpts (Wikipedia): - “Mary decides to sell the codicil to the Mompessons… More debts… Mary dies… John… salvation may lie in a second will… gets a job as a servant… Eventually John steals the will and flees.” (Part 4) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quincunx - “During a storm, John interrupts a secret marriage… in a derelict chapel at Mompesson hall.” (Part 5) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quincunx - Beat-by-beat: - (i) Protagonist in disguise: No; John becomes a servant in order to gain access (not a formal disguise beat). - (ii) Helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal: No; the story revolves around inheritance conflicts and wills. - (iii) Protagonist wrongly accused by the businessman of stealing a vital document: No; John actually steals a will (see Part 4 quote). - (iv) Villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad: No; secret wills/codicils are hidden within England. - (v) Climax with a fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist: No; there is a storm on land (chapel scene), not a sea storm; no businessman-rescue beat. Cross-title conclusions - None of the seven titles include all five emphasized beats. - Only A Spy in the House (Y. S. Lee) clearly includes (i) protagonist in disguise (infiltration “assuming the guise of a lady’s companion”) within a businessman’s household (merchant), per WorldCat: https://search.worldcat.org/title/1083452785 - No reliable-source evidence was found for: - (ii) the protagonist helping a businessman avert a disastrous deal; - (iii) the protagonist being wrongly accused by a businessman of stealing a vital document; - (iv) a villain scheming to send an encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad; - (v) a climax with a fierce sea storm where the businessman risks his life to rescue the protagonist for any of the seven works. Reliability notes and links used - Wikipedia (for detailed overviews and bibliographic confirmation): - The Quincunx (detailed chapter-by-chapter synopsis): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quincunx - The Wrecker (Stevenson novel): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wrecker_(Stevenson_novel) - The Last Dickens: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Dickens - Anne Perry (for title variant): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Perry - Library catalogs (WorldCat) for publisher summaries and publication data when Wikipedia pages were absent or minimal: - A Spy in the House (various records; key “guise” line): https://search.worldcat.org/title/1083452785 - A Spy in the House (Candlewick 2010): https://search.worldcat.org/title/863592991 - Treason at Lisson Grove (Ballantine, 2011): https://search.worldcat.org/title/651902112 - Treason at Lisson Grove (expanded summary): https://search.worldcat.org/title/1132252501 - Horatio Lyle (Atom, 2006): https://search.worldcat.org/title/67369661 - Mr. Meeson’s Will (assorted historical listings): https://search.worldcat.org/title/970930720 - Primary text (Project Gutenberg) for Mr. Meeson’s Will: - Main page: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11913 - Read online (chaptered HTML): https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/11913/pg11913-images.html - Example sea-voyage confirmation (opening of Ch. V). Limitations and uncertainties - Mr. Meeson’s Will: The novel is well-known for the shipwreck/tattooed-will episodes (post-wreck); while the primary text confirms the sea voyage (and, later in the novel, the island/tattoo plot), we did not surface a single secondary summary link explicitly stating “tattooed will at Kerguelen” during this session due to search constraints. The complete primary text (Gutenberg) provides full verification for readers. - None of the seven provided evidence for (ii)–(v) in the sense required by the task’s emphasized beats; if further confirmation is needed, deeper reading of full texts or additional scholarly/publisher synopses would be the next step. Conclusion Based on the collected authoritative sources (Wikipedia, WorldCat, and Project Gutenberg), none of the seven candidates match the five-beat plot template. The only confirmed overlap is (i) “protagonist in disguise” in A Spy in the House. No reliable evidence was found for the other specified beats in any of the seven works.

Final report: identification attempt, evidence collected, and conclusion Task recap - Goal: Name a historical fiction novel (published before 2017) set in 19th-century London that matches a specific five-beat plot: (a) protagonist in disguise; (b) helps a businessman avert a disastrous deal; (c) the businessman wrongly accuses the protagonist of stealing a vital document; (d) the true culprit is a schemer planning to send the encrypted/cipher/secret document abroad; (e) climax in a fierce sea storm where the businessman risks life to rescue the protagonist. Process summary (tools and steps used; no internal chain-of-thought) - Step 1: Ran a targeted web research task to surface and verify candidate novels combining disguise, London business/merchant themes, secret/cipher papers with foreign (abroad) stakes, and a sea-storm rescue climax. The research synthesized findings from reliable sources and returned a structured candidate list with beat-by-beat mapping and citations. - Step 2: Expanded the research to seven additional high-probability candidates (including YA historicals, Victorian mysteries, adventure classics, and modern Dickensian pastiches) and again mapped each against the five beats with citations (Wikipedia, WorldCat/publisher blurbs, Project Gutenberg where applicable). High-level outcome - No novel published before 2017 was found that clearly matches all five beats in one work. - Multiple partial matches were identified. Short stories (Sherlock Holmes) closely match the secret-document-to-foreign-agents beats, but they are not novels and lack the sea-storm rescue and businessman-rescues-protagonist elements. Candidates and evidence (mapped to beats and cited) A) Candidates from the initial research 1) The Shadow in the North (Philip Pullman, 1986; Sally Lockhart #2) - Setting/genre: Late 1878; London business/industrial intrigue; historical mystery (YA). - Evidence: - London and business intrigue; stolen files from a businessman’s house; weapons company conspiracy. - Citations: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shadow_in_the_North - Beat mapping: - (a) Disguise: Unclear. - (b) Business rescue: Partial (financial recovery for a client), not averting a businessman’s deal. - (c) Accused by businessman: No. - (d) Encrypted document abroad: No (industrial weapon scheme). - (e) Sea-storm rescue by businessman: No (fire/collapse set piece; rescued by allies). 2) David Copperfield (Charles Dickens, 1849–50; original Victorian) - Setting/genre: London and Yarmouth; bildungsroman. - Evidence: - Fierce sea storm with rescue attempt: “Ham … dies in a fierce storm off the coast while rescuing shipwreck victims. Steerforth … also dies.” - Citation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Copperfield - Beat mapping: - (a–d): No. - (e): Partial storm-rescue motif; rescuer is a fisherman, not a businessman; the protagonist is not the rescued party. 3) The Firm of Girdlestone (Arthur Conan Doyle, 1890; original Victorian) - Setting/genre: London merchant firm; business melodrama. - Evidence: - Diamond-mine hoax by businessmen; no secret-paper plot. - Citation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Firm_of_Girdlestone - Beat mapping: No on all five. 4) Armadale (Wilkie Collins, 1866; original Victorian) - Setting/genre: Sensation/mystery; includes maritime peril off Isle of Man. - Evidence: - Disguise/deception central to villain; a night on a shipwreck. - Citation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadale_(novel) - Beat mapping: - (a): Disguise present (villain), not protagonist in the specified sense. - (b–d): No. - (e): Maritime peril but not a businessman rescuing the protagonist in a sea storm. 5) The Meaning of Night (Michael Cox, 2006; historical crime) - Setting/genre: Victorian London; historical crime. - Evidence: - Protagonist uses multiple aliases/disguises: “Glyver (now masquerading as Edward Glapthorn)…” - Citation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Meaning_of_Night - Beat mapping: - (a): Yes (disguises). - (b–e): No. Short-story entries (format mismatch; included for overlap on secret papers) 6) The Adventure of the Naval Treaty (Arthur Conan Doyle, 1893) - Secret diplomatic document stolen; intended for foreign powers. - Citation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventure_of_the_Naval_Treaty - Beat mapping: (c)–(d) Yes; others No; not a novel. 7) The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans (Arthur Conan Doyle, 1908) - Stolen submarine plans; sale to foreign agents. - Citation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventure_of_the_Bruce-Partington_Plans - Beat mapping: (c)–(d) Yes; others No; not a novel. Additional Victorian/Victorian-set works noted for overlap 8) The Woman in White (Wilkie Collins, 1860) – Disguise/deception; lacks secret-docs-to-abroad and sea-storm rescue. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Woman_in_White_(novel) 9) The Moonstone (Wilkie Collins, 1868) – Theft and India link; no cipher-to-abroad; no sea-storm rescue. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moonstone 10) Fingersmith (Sarah Waters, 2002) – Cons/disguises in London; lacks secret-docs-abroad and sea-storm rescue. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingersmith 11) The House of Silk (Anthony Horowitz, 2011) – Holmes pastiche; London; not a secret-doc-abroad or sea-storm rescue story. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_House_of_Silk 12) The Way We Live Now (Anthony Trollope, 1875) – London finance scandal; lacks the specified beats. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Way_We_Live_Now B) Candidates from the expanded research 13) Mr. Meeson’s Will (H. Rider Haggard, 1888; adventure) - Setting/genre: England and at sea; shipwreck; tattooed-will plot. - Evidence: - Shipboard chapters and sea voyage on the “Kangaroo”; key document is a will, not a cipher. - Sources: Project Gutenberg (text): https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11913; HTML text: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/11913/pg11913-images.html; WorldCat record: https://search.worldcat.org/title/970930720 - Beat mapping: - (a): No evidence of disguise. - (b–d): No (document is a will; not encrypted or sent abroad). - (e): Sea peril present, but no businessman-rescues-protagonist storm climax per summaries. 14) A Spy in the House (Y. S. Lee, 2009; The Agency #1; YA historical mystery) - Setting/genre: Victorian London (1850s); espionage/infiltration. - Evidence: - “Assuming the guise of a lady’s companion, she must infiltrate a rich merchant’s home in hopes of tracing his missing cargo ships.” - Sources: WorldCat: https://search.worldcat.org/title/1083452785; https://search.worldcat.org/title/863592991 - Beat mapping: - (a): Yes (undercover disguise). - (b): Partial thematic alignment (merchant/cargo), but not a discrete “avert disastrous deal.” - (c–e): No supporting evidence found. 15) The Last Dickens (Matthew Pearl, 2009; historical/literary mystery) - Setting/genre: U.S., England, India; London included; Dickensian publishing intrigue. - Evidence: Quest to secure Dickens’s unfinished novel to save a business; not a cipher/abroad plot. - Citation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Dickens - Beat mapping: No on (a)–(e). 16) The Extraordinary and Unusual Adventures of Horatio Lyle (Catherine Webb, 2006; YA Victorian detective) - Setting/genre: London-based sleuthing; science/invention; YA. - Evidence: WorldCat summary emphasizes sleuthing; no secret-docs-abroad or sea-storm. - Citation: https://search.worldcat.org/title/67369661 - Beat mapping: No on (a)–(e). 17) Treason at Lisson Grove (Anne Perry, 2011; US title of Betrayal at Lisson Grove; Thomas & Charlotte Pitt) - Setting/genre: 1895 Special Branch; London, St. Malo, Dublin; political intrigue. - Evidence: Pursuit of assassin; informant; no cipher-to-abroad or sea-storm rescue elements. - Citations: Title variant confirmation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Perry;
